prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, transforming the analysis of exporting, reallocation across firms and the gains from trade

statement.case_for: My preferred part is unchanged. Melitz (2003) changed the unit of analysis in trade from the industry to the firm. Together with Helpman's work with Melitz and Yeaple on exporting versus foreign direct investment, it gives a selection margin with its own mechanism and its own testable predictions. Liberalisation raises aggregate productivity through reallocation toward more productive firms, and gains from trade have a within-industry channel that earlier models could not represent. These predictions have been examined on firm-level data from many countries for more than twenty years. The framework is the standard starting point for empirical and quantitative trade work. It also links to the reallocation and firm-dynamics literatures in growth, which is where I can judge it best. The two-name attribution is one of the cleanest on the shortlist, and the citation can be worded around the selection model so that it does not claim all firm-level trade research. I want the committee to weigh this against B001 on the criteria of originality, durability, breadth and cleanliness of credit, and not on opening support counts. On those criteria I see B001 as the main rival and B021 as a close, defensible alternative, not an obviously weaker case. My view of the merits has not changed since round 1. My view of the fallback has become firmer: if B021 stalls on the empirical-pioneer credit question, I would support Calvo, Taylor and Woodford in B001.
statement.case_against: The main reservation is credit. Bernard and Jensen documented the exporter facts first, and Eaton and Kortum built a parallel structural route to the gains from trade. None of them is on this entry, so a Helpman-Melitz prize would reward the theory of selection that organised those facts and leave out the people who first documented them. Melitz's contribution is concentrated in one seminal paper. The welfare conclusions depend on functional-form assumptions such as Pareto productivity. Some members will see the work as a continuation of the new trade theory recognised in 2008, and I treat that as a judgement the committee must make explicitly. B001 has the broadest opening support and a very large demonstrated influence on central-bank practice. If the committee puts policy reach ahead of attribution clarity, B001 is the natural choice and I would accept it. B001's attribution cost is also real, because the trio leaves out Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B001 first and B021 third. He says a Helpman-Melitz prize would leave out Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum, that it follows Krugman's 2008 prize, and that quantitative trade models may have partly absorbed the framework. He finds the monetary-policy framework more consequential and its credit somewhat easier to defend.
responses.response: I accept the credit gap, and it is my main uncertainty. I read supersession differently. Quantitative trade models keep the heterogeneous-firm selection margin and ask how much it matters for welfare, so the discovery is refined, not replaced. On B001, your origin-point argument for Calvo, Taylor and Woodford has persuaded me that this is the right trio, and I no longer favour a Galí-based set. I still disagree on 'easier to defend'. A trio that excludes Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets cuts through a larger group of near-equal claims than Helpman-Melitz does. That is a different problem from the Bernard-Jensen omission, which concerns who documented the facts. It is not a disagreement about who built the theory. So I do not move B001 ahead of B021 on attribution grounds. I do accept that it is ahead on breadth of policy use, and that is a judgement the committee can make either way.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B001 first with Taylor, Woodford and Calvo. He ranks B021 third, would support it if B001 stalls on attribution, and notes that the committee would have to frame a B021 citation around the selection theory. He also flags the dependence of welfare results on Pareto assumptions.
responses.response: I agree that the citation has to be framed around the selection model and gains from trade, and my drafted citation is worded that way. On the Pareto point, I think the sensitivity is real for the size of the gains. It does not affect whether the selection and reallocation margin exists, which is what the discovery rests on. Your menu-cost evidence on state dependence is relevant to B001 in the same way. A tractable device can be imperfect as a description and still be foundational. I apply the same standard to both candidates, so I do not count the Pareto sensitivity against B021 more heavily than the Calvo approximation against B001. Your statement that you would support B021 if B001 stalls is useful for the committee. I would support B001 under the same condition.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B001 first with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. He treats Redding as a follower and not a co-originator on B021, and he raises the Calvo-Taylor priority questions and whether the Taylor rule is science or policy prescription. He keeps Galí as a fallback if the committee wants a more empirical trio.
responses.response: On Redding we agree, and it supports a two-person B021. On B001 your origin-point logic moved me to the Calvo-Taylor-Woodford trio, and I am not reopening that. On the chair's question about the Taylor rule, I treat it as a scientific contribution when it is the object of positive analysis. That means its role in determinacy and in the evaluation of policy, not only its use as a prescription. I note that the Fischer and Phelps priority questions you raise cannot be resolved from the supplied entry. I read them as a drafting risk for the citation and not as a reason to doubt the core. We still differ on the weight of attribution risk. I count the excluded Galí-Gertler-Christiano-Eichenbaum-Smets group as a larger cost than the Bernard-Jensen-Eaton-Kortum gap, because the B001 omissions concern theory and estimation by people with near-equal claims. The B021 omissions are mainly about documenting and measuring the facts.

responses.point: The chair ranks B002 first with Kiyotaki and Moore. He concedes that the model is highly stylised, that direct empirical identification of the collateral channel comes mostly from later work by others, and that the 2022 prize may reduce novelty. He ranks B021 sixth because of the Krugman overlap.
responses.response: I take the clean two-author credit and the foundational status seriously. I treat the empirical caveat you state yourself as the deciding consideration for me. A prize for a stylised mechanism whose quantitative importance is disputed rests more on conceptual generality than on tested evidence. B021 has the opposite profile, because its predictions have been confronted with firm-level data across many countries. On Krugman, my view is unchanged. The 2008 prize addressed increasing returns and love of variety at the industry level, while this work concerns selection among firms, which is a different discovery. I accept that B002 is the cleanest macro attribution and that the committee could reasonably put it ahead of B021 on that criterion alone. I note your chair role and your co-authorship with me. I disclose it below and do not adjudicate it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges that crediting Helpman and Melitz alone leaves the prize incomplete because Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum are outside the entry, or accepts a citation confined to the selection model.
Whether the 2008 trade prize is read as covering the firm-heterogeneity line, which would make it a continuation and not a distinct step.

Whether B001's broader reach should outweigh its crowded attribution. If it does, I would accept Calvo, Taylor and Woodford, and my decision between B021 and B001 would turn on how the committee weighs the Galí-Gertler-Christiano-Eichenbaum-Smets omissions.
Whether the Pareto-based welfare sensitivity should be treated as a limit on the gains-from-trade claim or as a refinement.
My assessments rest on general knowledge and the supplied entries and openings. I have not independently verified citation counts, priority claims or adoption evidence.
statement.conflict_note: Disclosed, not adjudicated. No tie to Helpman or Melitz is apparent from my profile, and I have no recorded collaboration with any B001 credited name. I have long-running co-authorship with Peter Klenow (B050, not in my configuration). My frequent co-authors include committee members Per Krusell and John Hassler, who are not candidates, and I share IIES affiliation with both. I am an IIES colleague of Torsten Persson (B006), who is not in my configuration. My own research on firm dynamics, reallocation and misallocation is close in subject to B021, so I rely on the common criteria and the stated uncertainties. I have also helped with the Ekonomisk Debatt summaries of earlier prizes, which does not bear on any candidate here.
